newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stumps in two key battleground states.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stumps in two key battleground states.

text.p: President Bill Clinton reached out to independent voters in two key Midwestern battleground states on Tuesday by telling them they are better off than they were four years ago and urging them to "stay the course."

In campaign rallies in Illinois and Michigan, Clinton said that "compared to four years ago" the U.S. economy has 10 million new jobs and a lower jobless rate. His policies, he said, have led to a declining crime rate, fewer on welfare rolls and millions on the minimum wage about to get a raise.

He was particularly enthused by Justice Department figures from its annual victimisation survey that said 9.9 million people reported being victims of crime in 1995 compared to 10.9 million in 1994. The figure does not include murder.
Clinton's Republican challenger Bob Dole has attacked Clinton this week for pursuing weak policies against crime and illegal drugs.

At a rally at Homewood-Flossmoor High School in this Chicago suburb, Clinton called the crime victim numbers "good news for Americans," and at an earlier stop in the Detroit suburb of Westland, he said it was evidence that Americans should "stay the course" when they vote on Nov 5.
"I don't want to declare victory over crime. I just say we're heading in the right direction," he said.

His appeal was aimed at independent voters, the so-called Reagan Democrats. It was in 1980 that Republican Ronald Reagan picked up the support of traditional Democrats situated in suburbs of battleground states like Michigan, Illinois and Ohio.
Continuing another theme aimed at these voters, Clinton also pledged to continue his efforts to build what he called "the finest education system available to all Americans of all ages."

With seven weeks to go until election day, Clinton was attempting to solidify his already large lead over Dole in Illinois and Michigan, two Midwestern states that may hold the key to a race more experts predict will tighten.

Clinton's campaign received a blow earlier in Washington when the commission planning for the 1996 presidential debates recommended that Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and all other third-party candidates be excluded.

Asked by reporters if he would accept the recommendation, Clinton said he would leave the matter up to his debate negotiators, but he added: "I enjoyed having him (Perot) in there in '92. I thought he made a valuable contribution."

Asked whether he was afraid to debate Dole one-on-one, Clinton said: "I'm not afraid of any debate." Clinton's camp would have preferred that Perot be allowed to participate since he would seem more likely to draw voters from Dole rather than the incumbent Democrat.

Today's decision was met with regret by Clinton's lead debate negotiator Mickey Kantor. White House officials insisted Perot had a right to be included, particularly since his campaign qualified and received $29.2 million in federal money for the fall campaign.
"We'd like to see him in there," one official said. "He's on the ballot in every state. We gave him federal money."

But the decision did not dampen the enthusiasm of the president's high-flying campaign, basking in the glow of a lead in public opinion polls that has so far survived all of Dole's attempts to dampen it.
Clinton was on the first day of a four-day cross-country swing that was to take him to Chicago for the rest of the day, then to Arizona, Washington, Oregon and South Dakota the rest of the week.
